cls: Electrolyte replacement / maintenance solutions (sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium, magnesium, bicarbonate/phosphate)
pharm: Provide essential ions (Na+, K+, Cl-, Ca2+, Mg2+, HCO3-/PO4) to correct or prevent fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base imbalance.
quick: Individualized to the specific deficit and serum levels; oral ORS or IV solutions as indicated
Oral salts/ORS often taken with or after food to reduce GI upset
Generally safe when used to correct genuine deficits; individualize

summary: 'Electrolytes' refers to the family of products supplying essential ions - sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium, magnesium, bicarbonate, and phosphate - given orally (e.g., oral rehydration salts, potassium/magnesium supplements) or intravenously to correct or prevent disturbances of fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance. There is no single standardized FDA generic label; dosing is entirely individualized to the measured deficit, serum levels, renal function, and clinical context. The principal hazards are over-rapid correction (e.g., rapid sodium correction causing osmotic demyelination), and accumulation in renal impairment (hyperkalemia, hypermagnesemia, fluid overload). IV potassium in particular must never be given undiluted as a rapid bolus.
indications: Prevention and treatment of dehydration and electrolyte loss (e.g., oral rehydration in diarrhea/vomiting)
Correction of hyponatremia/hypernatremia, hypokalemia/hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatemia
Maintenance fluid and electrolyte therapy when oral intake is inadequate
Correction of metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate) where indicated

dosage.d: Reconstitute one sachet in the stated volume of clean water; give frequent small amounts titrated to ongoing losses and hydration status
dosage.n: Standard ORS ~75 mmol/L sodium, ~20 mmol/L potassium, glucose ~75 mmol/L

dosage.d: 20-40 mmol/day oral potassium chloride in divided doses, guided by serum K+
dosage.n: Take with food; IV only if oral not feasible

dosage.d: Typically up to 10 mmol/hour peripherally (higher only with central access and cardiac monitoring); never as an undiluted bolus
dosage.n: Must be diluted; rapid bolus can be fatal

dosage.d: 1-2 g IV over 15-60 minutes (or per protocol), guided by serum Mg2+ and renal function
Individualized; limit correction to no more than ~8-10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination
dosage.n: Use hypertonic saline only for severe symptomatic cases per protocol

admin: Always individualize to the measured deficit, serum levels, renal function, and ongoing losses
Dilute IV potassium and infuse slowly with cardiac monitoring; never give undiluted KCl as a rapid IV push
Correct sodium disturbances slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination (overly rapid hyponatremia correction) or cerebral edema
Reconstitute ORS in the exact stated volume of clean/boiled cooled water; do not add extra sugar or salt
Recheck serum electrolytes during correction and adjust the rate accordingly
moa: Electrolytes are the body's essential mineral ions. Sodium and chloride are the major extracellular ions governing extracellular fluid volume and osmolality; potassium is the major intracellular cation determining resting membrane potential and cardiac/neuromuscular excitability; calcium and magnesium are essential for neuromuscular conduction, enzyme function, and cardiac stability; bicarbonate and phosphate are key buffers in acid-base balance. Replacement products supply these ions to restore normal concentrations, correcting the cellular electrical, osmotic, and metabolic disturbances caused by their deficiency or excess.

absolute: Hypermagnesemia / significant heart block (for magnesium products)
Severe renal failure with anuria (for fluid/potassium/magnesium loads)
Fluid overload states for high-sodium/volume products
relative: Heart failure / cirrhosis with edema (sodium and fluid load)
Digoxin therapy (calcium and potassium shifts affect toxicity)
monitor: Serum electrolytes and renal function during correction
ECG for potassium, magnesium, and calcium disturbances
Fluid balance and signs of overload

preg: Correcting genuine electrolyte and fluid deficits is appropriate and generally safe in pregnancy; the specific agent and amount should be individualized. Magnesium sulfate is used therapeutically in eclampsia/pre-eclampsia under specialist care.
lact: Replacement of physiologic electrolyte deficits is compatible with breastfeeding; the ions are normal milk constituents. Individualize the product and dose.
renal: Renal impairment markedly raises the risk of accumulation - especially hyperkalemia, hypermagnesemia, hyperphosphatemia, and fluid overload. Reduce doses, monitor serum levels and ECG closely, and avoid potassium/magnesium loads in oliguric or anuric patients.
hepatic: In cirrhosis with ascites/edema, sodium and large fluid loads can worsen fluid retention. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia are common and may precipitate or worsen hepatic encephalopathy - correct carefully.

major: Potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs - with potassium products cause hyperkalemia
Digoxin - hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia potentiate toxicity; rapid IV calcium can precipitate fatal arrhythmia in digoxin toxicity
moderate: Loop/thiazide diuretics - increase losses of potassium and magnesium (may need replacement)
Corticosteroids - promote sodium retention and potassium loss
Quinolone/tetracycline antibiotics, bisphosphonates, levothyroxine - calcium/magnesium impair their absorption (separate dosing)
minor: Sodium bicarbonate alters urinary pH and renal excretion of some drugs
interactions.food: Oral salts/ORS are often taken with or after food to reduce GI upset; do not add extra sugar/salt to ORS.
interactions.alcohol: Chronic alcohol use predisposes to hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia, and hypophosphatemia - replacement is often needed.
interactions.diagnostics: Therapy directly changes serum electrolyte assays; bicarbonate affects blood gas/pH measurements.

serious: Osmotic demyelination from over-rapid sodium correction
rare: Tissue necrosis from extravasation of concentrated solutions (e.g., calcium, potassium)
emergency: Cardiac arrest from rapid/concentrated IV potassium
Acute pulmonary edema from volume overload

monitoring: Serum electrolytes (Na, K, Cl, Ca, Mg, PO4) and renal function during correction
ECG when correcting potassium, calcium, or magnesium
Fluid balance, weight, and signs of overload
counsel: Take oral electrolyte salts or ORS exactly as directed; mix ORS sachets in the stated amount of clean water only
Drink rehydration solution in frequent small sips, especially if vomiting
Tell your doctor about kidney or heart problems and all your medicines (some raise potassium)
Do not take extra potassium or salt substitutes without advice
Attend blood tests so your doctor can check your salt levels
pk: Oral absorption within minutes to hours; IV is immediate
Depends on the ion, route, and rate of administration
Not a classical drug - ions are handled by normal homeostatic mechanisms (renal/cellular)
Maintained by renal regulation; ongoing losses require continued replacement
Store solutions/sachets at controlled room temperature; keep reconstituted ORS no longer than 24 hours (refrigerated)
pearls: No single FDA generic label - 'electrolytes' is a class of replacement products (ORS, KCl, CaCl2/gluconate, MgSO4, NaHCO3, phosphate); guidance from BNF/WHO/clinical references, not openFDA
NEVER give undiluted IV potassium as a rapid bolus - it can cause fatal cardiac arrest
Correct sodium SLOWLY (about 8-10 mmol/L/24h) - too-rapid correction of hyponatremia causes osmotic demyelination
In renal failure, potassium and magnesium accumulate - check levels and ECG before and during replacement
Reduced-osmolarity WHO ORS is the standard for diarrheal dehydration; mix in clean water without adding sugar/salt
missed: For oral replacement, take a missed dose when you remember unless it is nearly time for the next dose; do not double up. For ongoing rehydration, simply continue replacing losses. IV electrolytes are managed by clinical staff against blood results.
overdose: Overdose depends on the ion: excess potassium causes hyperkalemia with peaked T waves, arrhythmia, and cardiac arrest; excess magnesium causes weakness, hyporeflexia, hypotension, respiratory depression, and heart block; excess sodium/fluid causes overload and pulmonary edema; excess calcium causes hypercalcemia. Management includes stopping the source, supportive care, and specific measures (e.g., IV calcium, insulin/glucose, and dialysis for hyperkalemia; IV calcium and supportive ventilation for hypermagnesemia; diuresis/dialysis for overload).
